description_ru: Научно-популярный текст о том, как иммунная система запоминает возбудителей и почему вакцины работают без болезни.
text:
Every day, your body is attacked by thousands of organisms that would like to use it as a home. Most of them are stopped before you notice anything. The reason is the immune system, a complex network of cells, tissues and chemicals that has been described, not unfairly, as an army with its own police force, its own factories and its own memory. Vaccines work by taking advantage of that memory, and understanding how they do it explains why they are among the most successful medical inventions in history.

The story begins in 1796, when an English doctor named Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease, seemed to be protected from smallpox, which killed millions of people. He tested his idea by infecting a boy with cowpox material and later exposing him to smallpox. The boy did not fall ill. Jenner did not know why, because bacteria and viruses had not yet been discovered, but his method was so successful that it was named after the Latin word for cow, vacca.

To understand the science, it helps to know what the immune system looks for. Every germ carries molecules on its surface that are called antigens. When an antigen enters the body, white blood cells recognise it as foreign. Some of these cells, called B cells, produce antibodies, which are small proteins shaped to fit a particular antigen, much as a key fits a lock. Antibodies attach themselves to the invader and mark it for destruction, or stop it from entering human cells.

Other cells, known as T cells, play a different role. Some of them attack infected cells directly, while others coordinate the response and tell the rest of the army what to do. The difficulty is that this process is slow the first time. It may take a week or more to produce enough antibodies, and during that period a dangerous virus can multiply rapidly. By the time the defence is ready, the person may already be seriously ill.

This is where memory comes in. After an infection, a small number of B and T cells survive as memory cells, and they can remain in the body for years or even for life. If the same germ returns, these cells recognise it at once and launch a much faster and stronger attack, often within hours. In most cases, the person never feels sick. A vaccine is simply a way of creating this memory without the illness that normally produces it.

There are several ways of doing this. The oldest method uses a weakened form of a germ, which can still trigger a response but cannot cause serious disease. Another uses a germ that has been killed, or only a harmless piece of it, such as a protein from its surface. More recently, scientists have developed vaccines that contain a set of instructions written in messenger RNA. The instructions are delivered into a few of the body's cells, which temporarily produce a single harmless protein. The immune system sees it, learns to recognise it and builds memory, while the instructions themselves break down within days.

Many people worry that a vaccine can overload the immune system. In fact, the opposite is true. A baby's body meets an enormous number of antigens every day simply by breathing, eating and crawling on the floor, and the antigens in vaccines are only a tiny fraction of that. A sore arm, a slight fever or tiredness are common reactions, and they are usually a sign that the immune system is doing exactly what it was designed to do.

Vaccines also protect people who have not been vaccinated. When a large proportion of a community is immune, the germ has difficulty finding new victims, and outbreaks fade away. This effect is called herd immunity, and it is especially important for those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies or patients with weak immune systems. The percentage needed depends on how contagious the disease is. For measles, which spreads extremely easily, about ninety-five per cent of people must be immune to stop it from circulating.

The results have been remarkable. In 1980, the World Health Organization declared that smallpox had been eradicated, the first and so far the only human disease to be completely wiped out. Polio, which once paralysed hundreds of thousands of children every year, has been reduced by more than ninety-nine per cent since the 1980s. Nevertheless, protection is not perfect, and some germs, such as influenza, change so quickly that new vaccines have to be designed every year.

In the end, a vaccine is not magic. It is a lesson. It shows the immune system a picture of the enemy before the real battle begins, and the body, being an excellent student, remembers. That simple idea, which began with a country doctor and a few milkmaids, continues to save an estimated several million lives every year.

questions.question: Who first used cowpox to protect against smallpox?
questions.answer: Edward Jenner, an English doctor, in 1796.

questions.question: What are antibodies?
questions.answer: Small proteins shaped to fit antigens and mark invaders for destruction.

questions.question: What is herd immunity?
questions.answer: When most of a community is immune, so the germ cannot spread easily.

questions.question: Which disease has been completely eradicated?
